title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
This page continues the 'Lemmata' of E449 for the residues of the powers a^0, a^1, a^2, ... modulo a prime P, with 0 < a < P.

§19 (end of proof). Claim: the first residue to recur is always 1. Suppose ε = residue of a^μ recurs first, at a^{μ+ν}. Then P | a^μ(a^ν − 1). Since a < P, a is prime to P, so P does not divide a^μ. Hence P | a^ν − 1 (tacitly Euclid's lemma). So a^ν ≡ 1 at an exponent ν < μ+ν, and 1 recurs before ε. This is cancellation in (Z/PZ)*: the power sequence is purely periodic, not merely eventually periodic.

§20. Once 1 reappears at a^ν, the next residue is that of a^{ν+1} ≡ 1·a ≡ a, using §5 (residue of a product is the product of residues). By induction the sequence 1, α, β, γ, ... repeats with period ν.

§21. Euler has defined a primitive root (§18) as an a whose residue series is 'complete', i.e. contains all of 1, ..., P−1. For such a, the P−1 distinct residues come from 1, a, ..., a^{P−2}. So a^{P−1} must repeat an earlier residue, and by §19 that residue is 1. Hence a^{P−1} ≡ 1.

§22 (statement only; the proof is on the next page). If the series is incomplete, the number r of distinct residues (the multiplicative order of a) divides P−1. The next page proves this by a coset argument: if 𝔄 is a non-residue, then 𝔄 times each residue is also a non-residue. These r new non-residues are distinct, and repeating the step shows P−1−r is a multiple of r. This is Lagrange's theorem for the cyclic subgroup ⟨a⟩ in (Z/PZ)*.

Purpose: an elementary 'group-theoretic' proof of Fermat's little theorem (§23). It also prepares the attempted proof (later in the paper) that primitive roots exist for every prime.
errors: §19 tacitly uses Euclid's lemma (a prime dividing a product divides a factor). This is standard and not a real gap.
§19's comparison 'a^ν inferior to a^{μ+ν}' needs μ ≥ 1. The case μ = 0 is trivial (ε = 1), so there is no real error.
No mathematical errors on this page. (The well-known gap in E449 concerns the later existence proof for primitive roots, not these lemmas.)

ideas.what: Powers of a unit mod p are purely periodic; the first repeated residue is 1 (cancellation)
ideas.modern_name: cancellation in the group (Z/pZ)*; pure periodicity of a^n mod p
ideas.where_published: E262 'Theoremata circa residua ex divisione potestatum relicta' (Novi Comm. 7, 1761); E449 (Novi Comm. 18)

ideas.what: Primitive root defined as a base generating all nonzero residues; a^{p−1} ≡ 1 for such a
ideas.modern_name: primitive root / generator of the cyclic group (Z/pZ)*
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, who introduced the term 'radix primitiva' in E449; existence was proved by Gauss (Disquisitiones, 1801)

ideas.what: Order of a divides p−1 (statement here, coset proof on the next page)
ideas.modern_name: Lagrange's theorem for the cyclic subgroup ⟨a⟩; order of an element divides the group order

deep.surprise_reason: These are standard lemmas toward Fermat's little theorem via orders and cosets. They are well documented in Euler's E262 and E449, and in histories such as Weil's and Sandifer's. Nothing on this page is new.
transcription_corrections: §20: 'sequens residuum erit α, 1 (5) = a' should read roughly: the next residue is that of a^{ν+1}, i.e. 1·a = a by §5, which is α. In this phrase the printed symbols (Greek α vs Latin a, and the sign) are ambiguous in the scan, so the reading is uncertain.
§21: 'ex totidem ergo progressionis geometricae terminis' matches the image, where 'ergo' is hyphenated across the line break.
